11. In motor learning and control, “heuristics” refer to simplified strategies or “rules of thumb” that the nervous system uses to make perception, decision‑making, and movement more efficient. Instead of processing every possible piece of sensory information in full detail, the system selects and prioritizes key cues (for example, focusing on the position of an object rather than its color when reaching for it). These shortcuts reduce computational load and speed up responses, but they can also bias performance. For instance, an athlete might rely on a learned heuristic for predicting a ball’s trajectory that works in most situations but fails under unusual spin or lighting conditions. Heuristics therefore represent a trade‑off between efficiency and accuracy: they support fast, generally effective action, yet can lead to systematic errors when conditions differ from the contexts in which they were learned.  

12. Group therapy operates on both individual and collective processes, and its effectiveness is best understood through the interplay of several key therapeutic factors. First, the group itself functions as a social microcosm: members bring their typical interpersonal patterns into the group, allowing these patterns to be observed, experienced, and modified in real time. Through feedback and interpersonal learning, clients become aware of how their behavior affects others and can experiment with new ways of relating in a safe environment. Second, cohesion—the sense of belonging, acceptance, and trust within the group—plays a role analogous to the therapeutic alliance in individual therapy; higher cohesion is associated with better outcomes because it facilitates openness, risk‑taking, and engagement in therapeutic tasks. Third, universality and normalization reduce isolation and shame: hearing others describe similar struggles helps members feel less alone and more hopeful. Additional mechanisms such as catharsis (emotional expression), altruism (helping others), and instillation of hope also contribute. Together, these processes create a setting in which clients both receive support and are challenged to grow, making group therapy particularly powerful for problems that are interpersonal in nature.
